t: Qohelet: the Gatherer, the Teacher, the Preacher
p: A title more than a name: one who gathers an assembly, or gathers sayings.
b: Qohelet comes from qahal, 'assembly' (the verb is 'to call together'). It is a feminine participle, a form Hebrew uses for offices, like soferet, 'scribe' (Ezra 2:55). So it is probably a title: 'the one who gathers', either a crowd to teach it or sayings into a collection (12:9). Once it has the article, 'the Qohelet' (12:8), and once it takes a feminine verb (7:27). The Greek translated it Ekklesiastes, 'a member of the assembly' or 'one who speaks in it', from ekklesia; that is the book's Greek and English name. Jerome's Latin Concionator and Luther's Prediger gave 'the Preacher' (KJV); many modern versions say 'the Teacher'. Both are guesses at the office. The site keeps the Hebrew word as a name, as many recent commentators do, so readers do not import a church preacher or a classroom.

t: Who speaks in the first verse?
p: A narrator introduces Qohelet and speaks about him; Qohelet himself begins only at 1:12.
b: The title talks about Qohelet in the third person, and so do 1:2, 7:27 and the epilogue (12:8–14). Everywhere else Qohelet says 'I'. Many scholars, following Michael Fox, call this outer voice the 'frame narrator': a second writer, or the author stepping back, who presents Qohelet's words, praises him as a sage (12:9–10) and adds the final charge to fear God (12:13). Others think the frame is the work of later editors who made the book safe for Scripture. Traditional readers take the frame as Solomon's own way of introducing himself. However one decides, the book is built as a report: someone hands us Qohelet's words and invites us to weigh them. See the book's opening pages.

p: The words fit Solomon, but his name is never used, and later verses fit a teacher better than a king.
b: Only Solomon among David's sons was king in Jerusalem, and 1:12–2:11 describes his wisdom, building and wealth (1 Kings 3:12; 1 Kings 4:29–34; 1 Kings 10:14–29). So Jewish and Christian tradition took Qohelet to be Solomon; the rabbis said he wrote the Song of Songs in youth, Proverbs in middle age and Ecclesiastes in old age (Song of Songs Rabbah 1:1). But the book never says 'Solomon', 'son' can mean any descendant of David, and after chapter 2 the speaker writes as a subject who watches kings from below (4:13–16; 8:2–4; 10:20). Most scholars, Jewish and Christian, now read the royal voice as a literary role, a teacher trying on Solomon's life to test what it gives. The Greek adds 'of Israel' after 'king' (see the variant).

p: Hevel is a breath or puff of vapor: real, but brief and impossible to hold. 'Vanity' and 'meaningless' are interpretations.
b: Hevel means breath, the mist of breath on a cold day, a puff of smoke. It is the name Abel, the brother whose life was short (Genesis 4:2), and elsewhere it means a human life (Psalm 39:5; Psalm 144:4) and empty idols (Jeremiah 2:5). 'Vapor of vapors' is the Hebrew way of saying 'the thinnest of vapors' or 'utter vapor', like 'holy of holies'. The KJV's 'vanity' comes from Jerome's Latin vanitas, 'emptiness', and the Greek mataiotes; today 'vanity' sounds like pride in one's looks. 'Meaningless' and 'futile' say that nothing matters, which is more than Qohelet always means. Scholars propose 'absurd' (Fox), 'fleeting' or 'transient', 'enigmatic' (Ogden and others), and 'beyond human grasp' (Seow, who keeps 'vanity' in his translation). Douglas Miller argues for 'vapor' itself, one symbol with three senses: what is insubstantial, what is fleeting and what is foul. This site follows his reading. The Plain keeps 'vapor' in all 38 places so readers can see the same word each time and judge what it means there: brief, empty, beyond grasp, or all three.
r: Genesis 4:2; Psalm 39:5; Psalm 144:4; Jeremiah 2:5; 12:8; Romans 8:20; James 4:14

p: The same cry returns in 12:8, so the whole book sits between two statements of it.
b: The narrator's 'Vapor of vapors... everything is vapor' comes back almost word for word at 12:8, just before the epilogue. Qohelet's words are placed between these two lines, the way a picture sits in a frame. 'Everything' (hakkol, 'the all') is one of his favorite words; it may mean every human effort, or the whole world as people experience it. The Greek translator's word for hevel, mataiotes, is the word Paul uses when he says the creation was 'made subject to emptiness' in hope (Romans 8:20), and many Christian readers hear Qohelet in that verse.

p: A business word: profit, surplus, the balance left after the costs are paid.
b: Yitron occurs only in Ecclesiastes (ten times), and the related words yoter and motar also mean 'more, advantage'. It comes from a root meaning 'remain, be left over'. In later Hebrew it is a trader's word for profit. Qohelet asks the accountant's question about a whole life: when the books are closed at death, what is left? His answer is that there is no lasting gain (2:11), though there can be a relative advantage, as light has over darkness (2:13). Many scholars see the language of a money economy behind such words, which fits the Persian period, when coins and trade spread through Judea (Seow).

p: The word joins work with trouble: the effort, the weariness and what it earns.
b: 'Amal (noun and verb) appears about 35 times in Ecclesiastes. Elsewhere it often means 'trouble' or 'misery' (Job 5:7; Psalm 90:10), and in Ecclesiastes it can mean the work itself, the strain of it, or its fruits (2:18–19, where one leaves one's 'toil' to an heir). The Plain keeps 'toil' everywhere, for noun and verb, so readers can hear the repeated 'all his toil that he toils'. The word is a key to the book's question: is human work worth its cost?

p: Found 29 times in Ecclesiastes and nowhere else in the Bible, but known from Phoenician tomb inscriptions.
b: The phrase means 'in this world, among the living'. It is not found elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible, but it appears in the Phoenician burial inscriptions of King Tabnit and his son Eshmunazar of Sidon (about 500–450 BC), which curse a grave robber to have no offspring 'among the living under the sun'. Greek poets likewise call the living those who see the light of the sun. So it was a common Near Eastern idiom in the Persian age. Ecclesiastes also says 'under the heavens' (1:13; 2:3; 3:1) with the same sense. Qohelet uses the phrase to mark his limits: he reports what can be seen in this life, not what God sees.

p: Generations, sun, wind and streams all move and return, and nothing is gained by it. Is that weariness, or order?
b: The poem (1:4–11) sets human life against the world. People pass, the earth stays. The sun, the wind and the streams go round and round. Most readers hear tiredness: all this motion achieves nothing, as human toil achieves nothing (1:3, 8). Others hear stability: the world is reliable, as in Psalm 104 and Genesis 8:22, and the contrast is with the short life of each generation. Ibn Ezra read the poem through the four elements of ancient science: the earth (1:4), the sun's fire (1:5), the wind, which is air (1:6), and water (1:7). The earth is the one that stays, the mother from which all things come and to which they return (compare Genesis 3:19). The poem's point is in 1:9–11: the world repeats, and people forget. Many think the poem is Qohelet's own; some think the narrator placed it as an overture.

a: it pants its way back to its place
p: The verb is used of a runner gasping for breath, or a person panting with desire.
b: Sho'ef means 'pant, gasp' (Isaiah 42:14, a woman in labor; Jeremiah 2:24, a wild donkey sniffing the wind). Some take it as 'longs for' or 'hurries'. Psalm 19 pictures the sun coming out 'like a bridegroom from the wedding room' and delighting 'to run the track' (Psalm 19:5). Qohelet takes the same image and turns it around: here the runner is out of breath, and the race never ends. The Greek has 'drags' (helkei), perhaps reading a similar verb.

p: The word ruach means wind here; in 3:19–21 it means breath or spirit.
b: The Hebrew does not name the subject until the middle of the verse: 'Going south and turning north, turning, turning goes the wind.' Hearers might at first think of the sun from 1:5 (the Greek joins the end of 1:5 to this verse), and only then learn it is the wind. Ruach is the same word that means 'breath' and 'spirit'. In this book it is usually 'wind', as in 'chasing the wind' (1:14), but in 3:19–21 and 12:7 it is the breath of life, and the note there takes up the question. Jesus' saying that 'the wind blows where it wants' (John 3:8) uses the same double sense in Greek.

a: and still the sea is not full
p: Ancient thinkers asked the same question; rabbinic readers thought the water returned under the earth.
b: Qohelet does not explain the cycle; he uses it as a picture of endless motion without result. Later readers explained it. Some medieval Jewish commentators said the waters return to their sources through channels under the earth, the deep below (compare Genesis 7:11). Greek writers also asked why the sea does not grow, and Aristotle discusses it in his Meteorology (book 2). Modern readers think of evaporation and rain (compare 11:3; Job 36:27–28). None of this is the verse's concern. Its point is that the streams keep going and nothing is ever filled, like the eye and the ear in 1:8.

p: Devarim means both 'words' and 'things'; the line may mean speech is exhausted, or everything is wearying.
b: Kol-hadevarim yege'im can mean 'all things are weary' (or 'wearying'), summing up the poem, or 'all words are weary', leading into the next line: 'no one can say it all.' The Greek has 'all words' (logoi). The Plain follows that reading because the verse is about speaking, seeing and hearing, the three ways of taking in the world; but 'things' is just as possible, and both may be meant: the world's motion wears out the words that try to describe it. The eye and ear that never have their fill return in 4:8 and in Proverbs 27:20.

a: Nothing at all is new under the sun.
p: Not a claim that inventions never happen, but that human life keeps the same pattern and people forget.
b: The saying does not deny new tools or events. It says what is done and what happens follows patterns that have run before, so no one can claim a truly new gain (1:3), and the claim to newness only shows that people forget (1:10–11). Qohelet says it again in 3:15: 'Whatever has been already is'. Jewish readers met the line in a famous Talmud story: when Rabban Gamaliel spoke of wonders in the world to come, a student objected with this verse (Bavli Shabbat 30b). Augustine used 1:9–10 against Greek philosophers who taught that the same individuals and events would recur in endless cycles; Qohelet, he said, meant kinds of things, not the same persons coming back (City of God 12.14). Christian readers set the line beside God's promise of something new (Isaiah 43:19) and 'Look! I am making everything new!' (Revelation 21:5): what is not found under the sun may still come from God.

p: Le'olamim is the plural of 'olam, 'a very long time'; it is the word behind 'forever' in 1:4 and 3:11.
b: 'Olam means time beyond view, backward or forward: 'forever', 'of old'. The plural, 'ages', is found in older Hebrew too (1 Kings 8:13; Isaiah 26:4). Qohelet uses the same word for the lasting earth (1:4), for God's works (3:14), for the lack of lasting memory (2:16) and, most famously, for what God has put in human hearts (3:11, see the note there). The site renders it 'forever' or 'long ages' so that readers can follow it.

p: The words can mean people or events; either way, no memory lasts.
b: Ri'shonim and 'acharonim, 'earlier ones' and 'later ones', have masculine endings and could refer to people (the generations of 1:4) or, as Hebrew often uses the masculine for 'things', to events (1:9–10). Most modern translations choose people; the Plain keeps the openness of the Hebrew. Loss of memory is one of Qohelet's deepest griefs. It comes back for the wise man (2:16), for the poor wise man who saved a city (9:15) and for the dead (9:5).

a: I, Qohelet, was king over Israel in Jerusalem.
p: Qohelet begins to speak as a king. Was he Solomon, an exiled Solomon, or a teacher in a royal role?
b: The past tense 'was' puzzled early readers, since Solomon reigned until he died. The Targum tells that Solomon grew proud, was driven from his throne by Ashmedai, the king of demons, and wandered among the towns weeping, 'I, Qohelet, was king' (compare Bavli Gittin 68b). Others read 'was' as 'have been'. Critical scholars see a literary form: a king tells what he did and what he learned, as in Egyptian royal instructions and Akkadian writings in which a king narrates his deeds and gives advice (Longman). The royal story runs through 2:26; after it, the king's mask is set aside. On any reading the voice gives the experiment its force: if a king with everything finds no lasting gain, no one will.

p: Ecclesiastes speaks of God 40 times and never uses the name YHWH.
b: Qohelet always says 'elohim, usually with the article, ha'elohim, 'God'. He never uses Israel's covenant name YHWH ('the LORD'), never names Moses, the covenant or the exodus, and speaks of God as the Creator who gives, tests, judges and is not to be argued with (3:14; 5:2). Some think this marks a God who is distant; others that Qohelet speaks as a wisdom teacher addressing every human being, as Job and much of Proverbs do; and others that the book's piety is real but sober. The Plain renders it 'God' throughout.

p: 'Inyan is a late word for business or occupation; ra' can mean 'evil', 'bad' or 'unhappy'.
b: 'Inyan appears only in Ecclesiastes (eight times). It is a noun from the verb in the same verse, la'anot bo, 'to be busy with it', and there may be a play on the verb 'anah, 'to afflict, humble'. The task is the drive to search and understand. It is God's gift and also a burden, because the search never reaches the end (3:10–11; 8:17). 'Evil' here is not moral wickedness; it is what feels bad to the one who carries it. The Plain keeps 'evil task' wherever this pair of words returns (4:8).

t: Chasing the wind, not 'vexation of spirit'
p: Re'ut ruach probably means 'shepherding the wind' or 'desire for wind'; the KJV's 'vexation of spirit' is a guess.
b: Re'ut ruach (and ra'yon ruach, 1:17; 4:16) is a phrase found only in Ecclesiastes, usually after 'vapor'. Most take it from ra'ah, 'to herd, tend', so 'herding the wind', like Hosea's 'Ephraim herds the wind' (Hosea 12:1); others from the Aramaic re'ut, 'will, desire' (Ezra 5:17), so 'longing for wind'. The Greek has 'choice of wind' (proairesis pneumatos). The KJV's 'vexation of spirit' follows an older guess from a root meaning 'break'. In each case the image is an effort that can never catch what it goes after. The Plain renders both forms 'chasing the wind' everywhere.

a: The bent cannot be set straight
t: A proverb about what cannot be fixed
p: Qohelet quotes a saying, then uses it to mark the limits of wisdom.
b: The verse has the shape of a proverb and may be one Qohelet knew. It sums up his study (1:13–14): some things are twisted and cannot be put right, and some things are missing and cannot be counted in. In 7:13 he gives the reason: no one can straighten what God has bent (see 7:13). Rabbinic teachers applied the line to wrongs that cannot be undone (Bavli Chagigah 9a) and to the dead, who can no longer repent (Ecclesiastes Rabbah 1:15). The verb taqan, 'set straight', is rare and late; Qohelet uses it again for his own arranging of proverbs (12:9).

a: I have gained wisdom beyond all
p: Only David ruled Israel from Jerusalem before Solomon, so the phrase has long puzzled readers.
b: Taken of Solomon, 'all who were over Jerusalem before me' is odd: the only Israelite king before him in the city was David (2 Samuel 5:6–9). Traditional interpreters answered that it includes the Canaanite kings of the city, such as Melchizedek and Adoni-zedek (Genesis 14:18; Joshua 10:1), or the wise men of Jerusalem. Many modern scholars take it as a sign that the speaker is a later writer using a royal style, in which kings boast of surpassing all their predecessors, as Assyrian and Babylonian kings did. The same claim returns in 2:7 and 2:9.

p: Qohelet studies wisdom's opposite too; the Hebrew spells 'folly' here like the word for 'insight'.
b: Holelot, 'madness', is a late word found only in Ecclesiastes (also 2:12; 7:25; 9:3; 10:13). Sikhlut, 'folly', is spelled here with the letter sin instead of samekh, so that it looks like sekhel, 'insight'. That may be why the Greek reads 'parables and understanding' (see the variant). The point is that Qohelet's search was complete: he wanted to know wisdom by knowing its opposite. The same three words come back as a set in 2:12.

p: Ka'as is vexation or grief, and sometimes anger; it is what knowing more brings.
b: Ka'as can mean anger (7:9), grief (Psalm 6:7) or frustration (2:23). Qohelet does not say that wisdom is bad; he says that the more one sees, the more it hurts, because one sees what cannot be fixed (1:15). The second line, 'the one who adds to knowledge adds to pain', may be a common saying. The idea is near to the English 'ignorance is bliss', though Qohelet never chooses ignorance (2:13).

a: let me test you with joy
p: Qohelet talks to his own heart, and tests pleasure as a scientist tests a sample.
b: Qohelet addresses his heart as 'you', as if it were another person, a habit of his (1:16; 2:15). He does not throw himself into pleasure; he 'tests' it, keeping wisdom in charge (2:3, 9). So this is not a story of a man who lost himself in luxury and repented, as later readers often told it, but a controlled trial. The verdict comes first ('this too was vapor') and the evidence follows (2:4–11). Simchah, 'joy', is the word he will later commend as God's gift (2:26; 8:15; 9:7). What he rejects here is joy as a way to gain; what he commends later is joy as a gift received.

p: The verb is literally 'drag' or 'draw'; its sense here is uncertain.
b: Limshokh bayyayin 'et-besari is literally 'to draw my flesh with wine'. Suggestions include 'to cheer', 'to refresh', 'to stimulate' and 'to sustain', and some compare a later Hebrew use of the verb for being drawn into something. The rest of the verse makes clear that this was not drunkenness: his 'mind kept steering by wisdom'. He wanted to know what folly offers without becoming a fool. Proverbs warns that wine mocks (Proverbs 20:1); Qohelet later counts wine among God's gifts (9:7; 10:19). 'Flesh' means the body as a whole.
orig: למשוך ביין את בשרי (limshokh bayyayin ʾet-besari)

p: Houses, vineyards, gardens, fruit trees and water: the list recalls both Solomon and the garden of Genesis 2.
b: The list of 2:4–8 matches what 1 Kings tells of Solomon: his palace and the house of the forest (1 Kings 7:1–12), his cities and stores (1 Kings 9:15–19), his gold, his singers and his many wives (1 Kings 10:14–27; 1 Kings 11:3). It also echoes Genesis 2. God 'planted' a garden with every tree good for food and a river to water it (Genesis 2:8–10); Qohelet planted parks with every fruit tree and made pools to water them. Some scholars read this as a deliberate picture of a man trying to rebuild Eden by his own work (Verheij). Ancient kings also boasted of gardens, as Sennacherib did of his gardens and canals at Nineveh, and the Persian kings of their parks.
r: 1 Kings 7:1–12; 1 Kings 9:15–19; 1 Kings 10:14–27; Genesis 2:8–10; Song of Songs 4:13

p: Pardes is a Persian loanword, 'walled park', the word behind English 'paradise'.
b: Pardesim comes from Old Persian pairidaeza, 'an enclosure', the walled hunting parks and orchards of Persian kings and nobles. It appears in the Bible only here, in Nehemiah 2:8 ('the keeper of the king's park') and in Song of Songs 4:13. Greek borrowed it as paradeisos, and the Greek translators used that word for the garden of Eden (Genesis 2:8); from there it became 'paradise'. Because the word cannot be older than Persian contact, it is one of the clearest signs that the book's Hebrew dates from the Persian period or later, with pitgam, 'sentence', in 8:11.

p: Kings dug pools and channels to water gardens and cities.
b: Jerusalem had 'the King's Pool' (Nehemiah 2:14) and 'the pool of the king's garden' (Nehemiah 3:15), and Hezekiah dug a tunnel to bring water into the city (2 Kings 20:20). Three large reservoirs south of Bethlehem are called 'Solomon's Pools', though they are much later, probably from the Hasmonean or Roman periods. In a dry land, water turned into a forest was the clearest sign of a king's power and wealth.
r: Nehemiah 2:14; Nehemiah 3:15; 2 Kings 20:20; Song of Songs 7:4

a: I acquired slaves, men and women
t: Slaves, and slaves born in the house
p: 'Eved can mean servant or slave; bought workers and those born in the household were slaves.
b: 'Eved covers a court official, a servant and a slave; the site renders it by context. Here the king 'acquired' them, and 'children of the house' were slaves born to slaves in his household, like the servants 'born in his house' that Abraham led (Genesis 14:14; Genesis 17:12). Owning many slaves was a mark of a rich household in the ancient world, and Qohelet lists them with his cattle as property. The Bible's laws limited and regulated slavery in Israel but did not end it (Exodus 21:1–11; Leviticus 25:39–46).

a: the treasure of kings and of the provinces
p: A medinah is a province, the administrative word of the Persian empire.
b: 1 Kings says that Solomon received tribute from kings and governors (1 Kings 10:14–15, 25). The word medinah, 'province', is used for the districts of the Persian empire in Esther, Ezra and Nehemiah (Esther 1:1; Ezra 2:1; Nehemiah 1:3), and later for any district. The word is old (1 Kings 20:14–19), but it is common in the Persian-period books. Segullah, 'treasure', is a king's private store (1 Chronicles 29:3), the same word God uses for Israel as his 'own private treasure' (Exodus 19:5).
r: 1 Kings 10:14–15; 1 Kings 10:25; Esther 1:1; Nehemiah 1:3; 1 Chronicles 29:3; Exodus 19:5; 1 Kings 20:14–19

p: Shiddah veshiddot appears only here. The guesses include concubines, cupbearers and chests.
b: Shiddah veshiddot, a singular followed by its plural, is a Hebrew way of saying 'many, one after another' (compare Judges 5:30, 'a girl, two girls'). The word itself appears nowhere else. Many modern scholars connect it with shad, 'breast', and take it as 'woman' or 'concubine', since 'the delights of human beings' come just before and Solomon had 700 wives and 300 concubines (1 Kings 11:3). The Greek has 'a male cupbearer and female cupbearers', and Jerome's Latin has cups and jugs for serving wine. Medieval Jewish readers compared the later Hebrew sheddah, a chest or carriage. The Plain follows the most common modern reading and keeps the Hebrew pattern.

a: This was my share from all my toil.
p: A share or portion: what one is given to enjoy, not a lasting gain.
b: Cheleq is the word for a portion of land or of spoil (Joshua 18:7; Genesis 14:24), and for the LORD as the Levites' share (Numbers 18:20; Psalm 16:5). Qohelet uses it for what a person actually receives from life: the enjoyment that comes with the work. It is real but limited. Here he finds that the pleasure was his share, and in the next verse that it was no 'gain' (2:11). The difference between 'share' (what you get now) and 'gain' (what is left at the end) runs through the book (3:22; 5:18–19; 9:9).

p: The Hebrew is clipped and unclear: it may be about a king's successor, or about anyone who repeats the king's search.
b: Word for word the verse says: 'For what (is) the man who will come after the king? That which already they have done it.' Readings: (1) the king's successor can only repeat what has been done, so the king's experiment is final; (2) no one coming after the king could test life more fully, so his conclusions stand; (3) the successor will inherit and maybe ruin what was done (leading to 2:18–19). Traditional readers who took Qohelet as Solomon thought of Rehoboam (1 Kings 12). The Greek reads 'after the counsel', taking the consonants for 'king' as an Aramaic word for 'advice', and it ends with a singular verb, 'he did it' (epoiesen), where the Hebrew has 'they have done it'. Some scholars also think the two halves of 2:12 have been switched, since the second half fits after 2:11. The Plain stays close to the Hebrew.
orig: מה האדם שיבוא אחרי המלך (meh haʾadam sheyyavoʾ ʾacharei hammelekh)

a: wisdom gives a gain over folly
p: Qohelet affirms what the wise taught (2:13–14a), then shows its limit (2:14b–16).
b: Here Qohelet agrees with Proverbs: wisdom is like light, and the fool walks in the dark. Then he adds that one fate meets both. Readers have explained such turns in different ways. Some scholars find quotations: Qohelet cites the teaching of the schools in order to answer it (Gordis). Others find a real tension he leaves standing, because life shows both (Fox: Qohelet 'contradicts himself' on purpose to report the world honestly). Older critics such as Siegfried (1898) gave the wisdom sayings, the calls to joy and the pious lines to different later hands, but few hold this now. Traditional readers saw a dialogue between the voice of faith and the voice of doubt. All agree the turn is part of the book's method.

p: Miqreh means what happens to a person; in Qohelet it is death, which comes to all alike.
b: Miqreh comes from qarah, 'to meet, happen': Ruth 'happened' on Boaz's field (Ruth 2:3), and the Philistines wondered whether a plague was 'chance' (1 Samuel 6:9). It is not the Greek idea of Fate as a power that plans a person's life. In Ecclesiastes it means the end that meets everyone, wise and fool, human and animal: death (3:19; 9:2–3). The Plain uses 'fate' in that limited sense, and the verb 'meet' where the Hebrew has qarah (2:14–15).

a: Oh, how the wise man dies along with the fool!
p: Psalm 49 says the same: wise and foolish alike die and leave their wealth to others.
b: The cry of 2:16 is close to Psalm 49: 'Indeed, one sees wise people die. Fool and dullard perish together and leave what they own to others' (Psalm 49:10). The psalm then hopes that God will ransom the speaker from the power of Sheol (Psalm 49:15); Qohelet offers no such hope here, and turns to hatred of life (2:17) and to the problem of the heir (2:18–21). The thought that no one will remember the wise is especially sharp, since a teacher's hope was to be remembered by his words (compare Proverbs 10:7).

p: Qohelet says plainly what Job and Elijah felt. He does not stay there.
b: The Bible lets its speakers say they hate life or wish to die: Job (Job 3:11; Job 7:16; Job 10:1), Elijah (1 Kings 19:4), Jeremiah (Jeremiah 20:14–18). Qohelet's hatred is that of a person who has found that his work will not last and that death erases the difference between wise and fool. He does not act on it, and the chapter ends with the gift of eating, drinking and seeing good (2:24). Readers differ over his tone: some hear despair; others hear honest grief that clears the way for gratitude. When Jesus speaks of hating one's life (John 12:25), the sense is different: putting him first.

p: A rich man cannot choose what his heir will do with his work.
b: In the ancient world, as now, a man's estate passed to his heir, and there was no guarantee that the heir would be wise (2:19). Readers who took Qohelet as Solomon thought at once of Rehoboam, whose foolish reply to the people split the kingdom (1 Kings 12:1–19). But the point is general: toil builds something the toiler will not control. The theme returns with the man who has no heir at all (4:8) and the man whose wealth is lost (5:13–14).

a: made my heart give up hope
p: The verb means 'give up hope'; it appears in this form only here.
b: Leya'esh 'et-libbi means 'to make my heart give up hope', and the Plain keeps that. Elsewhere the related form means 'It is hopeless!' (Jeremiah 2:25; Isaiah 57:10). Qohelet 'turned around' to it: having looked at his works (2:11), he now looks at what will happen to them and gives up. This is the low point of the royal story. The next verses explain why, and 2:24 begins the turn.

p: Ra'yon is the same word as in 'chasing the wind' (1:17; 4:16).
b: Ra'yon libbo uses the word found in ra'yon ruach, 'chasing the wind'. So the striving of the heart is like chasing wind. The Plain keeps 'chasing' in both places to let readers hear the link. The next verse gives the result: pain by day and no rest by night.

a: There is nothing good for a person but to eat and drink and let himself see good in his toil.
p: The first of seven passages that commend eating, drinking and enjoying one's work as a gift from God.
b: The refrain returns six more times (3:12–13; 3:22; 5:18–20; 8:15; 9:7–10; 11:7–12:1), and Whybray called Qohelet a 'preacher of joy'. Others hear resignation: since there is no gain, take what pleasure you can (Crenshaw). The Hebrew literally says 'there is no good in a person that he eat...', and the Greek reads the same. Many scholars think a letter has dropped out ('than that he eat', as 3:22 has it), or that the comparison is simply left unsaid; the Plain's 'but' reads it that way without changing the Hebrew. Others take the Hebrew as it stands: it is not in a person's power to eat and enjoy, because that 'comes from God's hand'. The key is the last line: enjoyment 'comes from God's hand'. It cannot be produced by toil; it is given. Jerome added a spiritual sense, the food and drink of Christ's body and blood. Luther read the book as teaching people to use present gifts with thanks and without anxious grasping. Isaiah 22:13 and 1 Corinthians 15:32 quote a cynical 'Eat and drink, for tomorrow we die', but Qohelet's advice is set under God.
orig: אין טוב באדם שיאכל ושתה (ʾen tov baʾadam sheyyokhal veshatah)

p: The verb chush is uncertain: 'enjoy', 'worry' or 'hurry'. The Greek has 'spare'.
b: Chush usually means 'hurry' (Psalm 55:8). Some take it here as 'worry' and some as 'hurry to it', but many modern scholars compare a later Hebrew and Aramaic word for feeling and take it as 'enjoy', which pairs well with 'eat'. Rahlfs' Greek has 'who will spare', and Codex Vaticanus 'who will drink'. On 'apart from me', see the variant.

p: Chote' means one who misses the mark; in Qohelet it may mean someone out of God's favor.
b: Chote' is the usual word for a sinner, from a root meaning 'miss the mark' (Judges 20:16). Some scholars think that in Qohelet it means simply 'one who displeases God', the opposite of 'the one who is good in God's sight', without saying why God is pleased or not (Fox: 'the offender'). On this reading the verse says that God gives joy freely to whom he will, and the toil of others ends up in their hands, which is itself 'vapor'. Others take it morally, as in Proverbs 13:22, where the sinner's wealth is stored up for the righteous; and older critics thought the verse was a pious editor's addition. The last line, 'This too is vapor', applies to the whole arrangement.

p: Zeman is a late word for a set time; 'et is the common word for time, used 28 times in 3:2–8.
b: Zeman appears only in late books (Nehemiah 2:6; Esther 9:27, 31) and in Aramaic Daniel. It means an appointed time. 'Et is the ordinary word for a time or occasion. Chefets, 'matter', meant 'delight' in older Hebrew and 'affair, thing' in later Hebrew. So the opening line is: everything has a moment set for it. The poem then lists fourteen pairs. The Greek uses chronos and kairos, 'time' and 'the right moment'.

p: Fourteen pairs of opposites cover all of life. Is the point 'act at the right time', or 'you cannot control the times'?
b: The poem (3:1–8) names 28 times in 14 pairs, from birth to death and from war to peace, moving between good and bad. Pairs of opposites stand for everything between them. Readers have taken it three ways. (1) Practical wisdom: the wise person knows the right time to act and to speak (Proverbs 15:23; Proverbs 25:11). (2) Divine control: the times are set by God and come whether we choose them or not; the verses after the poem point this way (3:10–11, 14–15). (3) Acceptance: every season, even mourning and tearing down, has a place in a world God made beautiful 'in its time' (3:11). Jewish readers took several lines in specific ways (the stones in 3:5, the tearing in 3:7). The poem is one of the most read passages of the Bible, at funerals and weddings, and in 1959 Pete Seeger set it to music as 'Turn! Turn! Turn!'.

t: To give birth, not 'to be born'
p: Ledet is active: a woman gives birth. The KJV's 'to be born' changes the subject.
b: Ledet is the active form of yalad, used of a mother bearing a child, as in Genesis 4:1. The KJV and many later versions render it 'to be born', which makes the pair birth and death of the same person. Read actively, the line is about human acts, like all the other pairs: giving birth and dying, planting and uprooting. Some scholars think the familiar rendering still catches the sense, since the line frames a life; but the Hebrew names the mother's act.

a: a time to throw stones away and a time to gather stones
p: Clearing a field, spoiling an enemy's field, building, or a figure for marriage: the line's sense is debated.
b: The line is the only one in the poem whose meaning is unclear. Suggestions: farmers clear stones from a field and gather them for walls or houses (Isaiah 5:2); armies throw stones into an enemy's fields to ruin them (2 Kings 3:19, 25); merchants count with stones; or, because the next line is about embracing, a figure for marriage relations. That last reading is found in the rabbinic midrash on the verse (Ecclesiastes Rabbah 3:5). Since the poem pairs a line about objects with a line about people elsewhere too, any of these may be meant.

a: a time to tear and a time to sew
p: Mourners tore their clothes, and later custom mended them; silence also belongs to mourning.
b: In Israel a mourner tore his garment at news of death (Genesis 37:34; 2 Samuel 1:11; 2 Samuel 13:31) and, in later Jewish custom, mended it after the time of mourning. Jewish mourners still tear a garment (keri'ah). The next line may continue the scene: Job's friends sat in silence for seven days before they spoke (Job 2:13). Read this way, 3:7 describes the course of grief.

a: a time of war and a time of peace
t: Does the poem approve of killing and war?
p: The poem describes what happens in human life; it does not tell readers when to kill or to hate.
b: Some readers worry that 'a time to kill' (3:3), 'a time to hate' and 'a time of war' approve violence. Most commentators answer that the poem describes the range of human experience, which God allows and limits (3:11, 14), not a list of duties. The last two pairs reverse the order: love then hate, war then peace, so the poem ends on peace. Christian readers who argue about just war and pacifism rarely build on this verse, since it says nothing about which wars are right.

a: What gain is there for the one who does the work
p: After the poem of times, Qohelet repeats the opening question of 1:3.
b: If everything has its time and the times are not ours to choose, what does the worker gain? The question repeats 1:3 with the word yitron, and Qohelet answers it by turning to God's work (3:10–15). This turn from human effort to God's doing is the center of chapter 3.

a: He has also put forever in their hearts
t: 'Olam in the heart: eternity, the world, or ignorance?
p: One of the book's great puzzles. The word usually means 'forever'; others read 'the world' or 'darkness'.
b: The Hebrew is gam 'et-ha'olam natan belibbam. (1) 'Eternity, forever': 'olam normally means long or endless time (1:4; 3:14), and the Greek has ton aiona. God has given people a sense of time beyond their own moment, a longing to see the whole, though they cannot find out what God does 'from the beginning to the end'. (2) 'The world': in later Hebrew 'olam means 'world', and Jerome's Latin has mundum, 'the world'. Medieval Jewish readers took it as love of the world, or knowledge of it. (3) By changing only the vowels to 'elem, some scholars read 'hiddenness' or 'ignorance', from the root 'to hide': God has put darkness in the mind, so that people cannot find out his work. The Plain follows the usual sense, 'forever', which fits the 'forever' of 3:14. Many Christian readers have heard in it Augustine's 'our heart is restless until it rests in you' (Confessions 1.1).
orig: את העלם נתן בלבם (ʾet-haʿolam natan belibbam)

p: Yafeh is beautiful, but here also 'fitting, right for its moment'.
b: Yafeh is the ordinary word for beauty (Genesis 12:11; Song of Songs 1:15). Qohelet uses it for what is fitting (5:18). 'Everything he has made beautiful in its time' looks back to the poem: each time, even the hard ones, fits in God's ordering of the world. Many hear an echo of Genesis 1, where God sees that what he made is 'good'. The echo is not exact (the word there is tov), but the thought is close.

t: Do good, or have a good time?
p: La'asot tov can mean 'do what is right' or 'fare well, enjoy oneself'.
b: Most often 'to do good' is moral (Psalm 34:14; Psalm 37:3). But next to 'to be glad', and in a passage about eating and drinking (3:13), many scholars take it as 'to enjoy oneself, to fare well', like the English 'do well for oneself' (compare 7:14, literally 'in a day of good, be in good'). The Greek has 'to do good'. The Plain keeps the literal words so that both readings stay open. Either way, Qohelet commends the life lived now, not a gain saved for later.

a: There is no adding to it and no taking away from it.
p: The same formula guards the words of the Law in Deuteronomy; here it guards the works of God.
b: Deuteronomy says of the commands: 'Do not add anything to the word I am commanding you, and do not take anything away from it' (Deuteronomy 4:2; compare Deuteronomy 12:32; Revelation 22:18–19). Qohelet uses the same language for God's works: they stand as they are, and no one can improve them or undo them (compare 7:13). The purpose is reverence: God has acted 'so that people will fear him'. Fearing God is one of the book's few steady teachings (5:7; 7:18; 8:12–13; 12:13).

a: God seeks out what is pursued
p: Nirdaf means 'what is chased'; it may be the past that has fled, or the person who is persecuted.
b: The phrase is short and unclear. (1) Many modern scholars take it with the first half: what has been chased away, the past, God seeks it out and brings it back, so the pattern repeats (1:9). (2) The rabbis read it of persecuted people: God always takes the side of the pursued, of Abel against Cain, Noah against his generation, Israel against the nations (Leviticus Rabbah 27:5; Ecclesiastes Rabbah 3:15). (3) Some read it with 3:16–17: God will seek out what was done, to judge it. The Plain keeps the literal words.

a: wickedness was there in the place of judgment
p: Where the courts should give justice, there is wickedness.
b: The 'place of judgment' is the court, held at the city gate (Deuteronomy 21:19; Amos 5:15) or before royal officials. The prophets condemned corrupt judges (Isaiah 1:23; Amos 5:12). Qohelet does not preach against them; he reports what he has seen, as he will report oppression and the chain of officials in 4:1 and 5:8. Scholars who date the book to the Persian or Ptolemaic period point to the power of governors, tax collectors and local strongmen in those times.

p: The last word of the verse is 'there'. Where? With God, in the world to come, or a misread verb?
b: The verse ends with sham, 'there'. (1) 'There' with God, at the place and time of his judgment; many Jewish and Christian readers took it as a judgment after death. (2) Many modern scholars read the same letters as sam, 'he has set' (a change of the dot over the letter shin), so 'he has set a time for every deed'. (3) Others read it as 'there' in the world under the sun: God will judge within history, at the time he chooses. The Greek moves 'there' to the start of 3:18. The Plain keeps 'there' and leaves the place open.

a: on their own they are animals
t: Humans tested and shown to be animals
p: The Hebrew is hard: God 'sifts' people so that they see that by themselves they are like animals.
b: Levaram means 'to sort, purify, test' them (Daniel 11:35). Lir'ot is 'to see', or with other vowels 'to show'. Hemmah lahem means 'they, themselves' or 'they, to themselves'. So the sense may be: God tests people so that they will see that, considered on their own, they are animals; or so that God may show them this, as the Greek reads ('to show', tou deixai). Qohelet means the fact of death (3:19–20), not that humans lack reason or dignity. The Greek has 'about the speech of human beings', taking divrat in its sense 'word'.
orig: לברם האלהים ולראות שהם בהמה המה להם (levaram haʾelohim velirʾot shehem-behemah hemmah lahem)

p: The same ruach that is 'wind' in 1:6 is here the breath of life that humans and animals share.
b: Genesis says that all living things have 'the breath of the spirit of life' (Genesis 7:22), and Psalm 104 says of the animals: 'You gather back their breath, and they die and go back to their dust' (Psalm 104:29). Qohelet agrees. In what can be observed, human and animal breathe alike and die alike. That is why he asks in 3:21 who knows what happens to the breath, and why 12:7 can say that 'the spirit goes back to God, who gave it'.

a: Humans have no edge over animals
p: Qohelet speaks of death, not of worth. Elsewhere the Bible sets humans apart in the image of God.
b: Genesis 1:26–28 sets humans apart as made in God's image, and Psalm 8 says they were made 'a little less than God'. Qohelet's point is narrower: in death there is no difference. Psalm 49 says the same of the arrogant rich: 'he is like the animals that are silenced' (Psalm 49:12). Readers who take Qohelet as a skeptic hear a denial of any human distinction; most read the line as a statement about what death does, made to humble those who think wisdom or wealth will protect them (3:18). The word for 'edge', motar, is related to yitron, 'gain' (1:3).

a: Everything came from the dust, and everything goes back to the dust.
p: The line looks back to Genesis 2–3: made from dust, returning to dust.
b: The LORD God 'shaped the man from dust of the ground' (Genesis 2:7) and told him that he would go back to dust: "to dust you will go back" (Genesis 3:19). Job and the Psalms say the same (Job 34:15; Psalm 104:29). The 'one place' is the grave, or Sheol, the world of the dead where all go (6:6; 9:10). Qohelet applies the curse of Genesis 3 to animals and humans alike. The words are part of many Christian burial services ('earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust').

a: Who knows whether the spirit of human beings goes up above
t: Who knows whether the spirit goes up?
p: A key verse in debates about the soul. It is a question, and readers disagree about what Qohelet's answer was.
b: Qohelet asks whether anyone knows that the human spirit goes up and the animal's goes down. Some hear a denial: no one knows, so there is no basis for hope beyond death (Crenshaw; Fox). Others hear a challenge to a claim some people were making in his day, that human spirits rise to the heavens, a belief found in Greek thought and in some Jewish circles; Qohelet says no one can know it by observation (Seow). The Masoretic vowels keep the question but turn 'whether it goes up' into 'which goes up': 'who knows the spirit of human beings, which goes up above?' So the verse seems to assume that the human spirit rises, and Ibn Ezra and others read it that way (see the variant). Later Qohelet says that 'the spirit goes back to God, who gave it' (12:7). The verse, with 9:5 and 9:10, is used in arguments about the state of the dead; the chapter page sets out the traditions.

t: After him: after death, or after his time?
p: The phrase may mean what happens to him after death, or what happens on earth after he is gone.
b: Qohelet uses 'after him' for the future on earth after a person's death (6:12; 7:14; 10:14), and that is the likely sense here: no one can come back to see what becomes of his work and his heirs (2:18–19). Some readers take it as life after death, continuing 3:21. Either way, the advice is to be glad in one's work now, since that is one's 'share' (2:10).

p: 'Ashuqim are acts of extortion and abuse by the powerful; the oppressed have no one to comfort them.
b: 'Ashaq is to oppress or extort, often by withholding wages or seizing goods (Leviticus 19:13; Amos 4:1; Micah 2:2). Qohelet sees tears and power, and says twice that the oppressed have 'no one to comfort them'. Five times Lamentations says that ruined Jerusalem has no one to comfort her (Lamentations 1:2, 9, 16, 17, 21). Under Persian and later Ptolemaic rule, local officials and tax farmers held great power; Josephus tells of the tax farmer Joseph son of Tobiah, who collected the taxes of Judea and Syria with soldiers behind him (Antiquities 12.4). Qohelet names no names and calls for no revolt; he refuses to look away.

p: Greek poets said it was best not to be born; Job cursed his birth. Qohelet says it of the oppressed.
b: The Greek poet Theognis (500s BC) wrote that the best thing for mortals is never to be born, and the next best to die soon; Sophocles repeats it (Oedipus at Colonus 1224–1227), and Herodotus tells how the gods gave two young men an early death as the best gift (Histories 1.31). Job wished he had died at birth (Job 3:11–16), and Jeremiah cursed his birthday (Jeremiah 20:14–18). There is no sign that Qohelet borrowed from the Greeks; such thoughts come to people who see much suffering. The verb shabbach, 'praise', 'count happy', is late Hebrew. Qohelet does not stay here: by 9:4 he says, 'It is better to be a living dog than a dead lion'.
orig: ושבח אני את המתים (veshabbeach ʾani ʾet-hammetim)

a: it is rivalry between a person and his neighbor
t: Envy as the engine of work
p: Qin'ah is jealousy or competition. Hesiod made a similar point about 'good strife' among workers.
b: Qin'ah can mean zeal (Psalm 69:9), jealousy (Proverbs 6:34) or envy (Proverbs 14:30). Qohelet sees that much hard work and skill is driven by wanting to match or beat the neighbor. The Greek poet Hesiod, about 700 BC, said there are two kinds of strife, and the good kind makes the idle man work when he sees his rich neighbor: 'potter is angry with potter, and craftsman with craftsman' (Works and Days 11–26). Hesiod praised it; Qohelet calls it vapor. The next two sayings (4:5–6) give two ways out: the lazy fool and the quiet hand.

p: A proverb: the lazy fool ruins himself. Or he has enough to eat without work?
b: Folded hands are the lazy man's pose in Proverbs: 'a little folding of the hands to lie down' (Proverbs 6:10; Proverbs 24:33). 'Eating one's own flesh' usually means destroying oneself (Isaiah 49:26; Micah 3:3). So most read: the fool who will not work starves and ruins himself. A few take 'flesh' as 'meat' and read the saying ironically: the idle fool still has his meat. Then 4:6 sums up: one handful with rest is better than two fists full of toil. Qohelet seems to set two proverbs side by side, one against laziness and one against overwork, so that the reader finds the middle.

a: One hand filled with rest is better
p: One of many 'better... than' sayings, a form Proverbs uses and Qohelet makes his own.
b: Proverbs has many such sayings: 'A little, along with the fear of the LORD, is better than a big store of treasure with turmoil inside it' (Proverbs 15:16; compare Proverbs 15:17; Proverbs 16:8; Proverbs 17:1). Qohelet uses the form often (4:3, 9, 13; 7:1–10; 9:16–18). Here the contrast is between one open hand (kaf) and two closed fists (chofnayim), between nachat, 'rest, quiet', and 'toil and chasing the wind'.
orig: טוב מלא כף נחת (tov meloʾ khaf nachat)

p: The Hebrew shifts without warning from 'he' to 'I'; the Plain adds 'he asks' to mark the quotation.
b: In Hebrew the verse moves from 'there is one... his toil... his eye' straight into 'For whom am I toiling?' Some think Qohelet suddenly speaks of himself; most take it as the lonely man's own question, which he never stops to ask. The Plain marks it as a quotation. The man has no son and no brother, so no heir (compare 2:18–21), and his eye never has its fill of riches (1:8). The Hebrew text writes 'his eyes', but the Masoretes' reading note, and the verb, have 'his eye' (see the variant).

p: Partners at work, travelers on the road, friends and spouses: the sayings fit many settings.
b: The four pictures (4:9–12) are about work (a good wage), travel (falling on the road), sleep on a cold night, and defense against an attacker. They suit travelers or business partners as well as married couples, and the man of 4:8 who had no one. Genesis says, 'It is not good for the man to be by himself' (Genesis 2:18). Jewish and Christian readers have applied the verses to marriage and friendship, and monastic writers to life in community rather than alone. The point is practical: companionship is a real advantage under the sun, unlike the gains Qohelet has dismissed.

a: woe to the one who falls on his own
p: The Hebrew writes one odd word, ve'illo. Most read it 'woe to him'; a few take it as 'if'.
b: The written word is ve'illo. Most readers, ancient and modern, take it as 'i lo, 'woe to him' (compare 'i-lakh, 'woe to you', in 10:16), and the Greek has 'woe to him' (ouai auto). A few scholars compare the later Hebrew and Aramaic 'illu, 'if', and read 'but if the one who is alone falls...'. The sense is the same either way: whoever falls with no one beside him stays down. The verb in both halves is heqim, 'raise up', the word used for helping a fallen animal to its feet (Deuteronomy 22:4).

a: a thread twisted three times does not snap quickly
p: A proverb also found in a Sumerian Gilgamesh poem. Christians later read it of God in a marriage, or of the Trinity.
b: In the Sumerian poem Gilgamesh and Huwawa, Gilgamesh encourages his companion Enkidu with sayings about two together, among them that a three-ply rope is not easily cut. Aaron Shaffer pointed out this parallel in 1967, and many scholars see it as evidence that such proverbs circulated widely, perhaps through Gilgamesh, which was still copied in Qohelet's day. The jump from 'two' to 'three' is a common proverb pattern (compare Proverbs 30:15). Christian preachers have read the third strand as God in a marriage, and some early writers as the Trinity or faith, hope and love; these are applications, not the verse's first sense.

a: Better a young man who is poor and wise than a king who is old and a fool
p: A story told in a few lines. Readers have seen Joseph, David, the good impulse, or a ruler of Qohelet's own time.
b: The old king who will no longer be warned is replaced by a poor young man from prison, and then the crowds move on to a 'second' young man (4:15). Readers have suggested Joseph, who went from prison to power (Genesis 41:14, 41); David and Saul; Jeroboam and Solomon; or, among historical critics, later rulers of the Persian or Ptolemaic age, though no proposal has won agreement. The Talmud reads it inwardly: the poor wise child is the good impulse, and the old foolish king is the evil impulse, which comes first in a person and rules like a king (Bavli Nedarim 32b; Ecclesiastes Rabbah 4:13). Qohelet's point holds in any case: wisdom is better than power, but popularity does not last (4:16).

p: Beit hasurim is 'the house of the prisoners', with a short spelling. 'He' and 'his kingdom' are unclear.
b: Mibbeit hasurim is 'from the house of those bound', spelled without the first letter of 'asurim, 'prisoners'. Some have read it as 'the house of the rebels' (from sur, 'turn aside'), but most take it as prison. The second half is ambiguous: it may mean that the young man was born poor in the kingdom he came to rule, or that the old king, even while reigning, became poor. The Plain keeps the Hebrew's 'in his kingdom'.

a: the young man, the second one
p: The 'second' may be the old king's successor, or a third figure who replaces the young man himself.
b: Some readers take 'the second' as simply the second king, the young man who follows the old one. Others see a cycle: the crowd that cheered the young man soon turns to yet another successor, the 'second' young man (4:16). Some scholars remove 'the second' as a later addition, but the Greek has it. The cycle reading fits the book's theme: kings rise and are forgotten, as generations come and go (1:4, 11).

a: those who come later will not be glad in him
t: Who were before them, and who come later
p: The crowds may be those the young king led, or the generations before; either way the next ones forget him.
b: The first half is unclear. Lekhol 'asher-hayah lifneihem is literally 'to all that he was before them'. It may mean 'all whom he led', the crowds the young king went before, or 'all who were before them', the earlier generations, set against 'those who come later' in the next clause. The Greek reads 'all who came before them', and the Plain follows that sense. Either way, there is 'no end' to the people, as there is 'no end' to the lonely man's toil (4:8). Yet later generations will not be glad in him. Qohelet's readers, who lived under kings whose favor rose and fell, would recognize the pattern. The chapter that began with the tears of the oppressed ends with the people's fickle praise, and both are 'vapor and chasing the wind'.
